text:
Pittsburgh had more of the puck. Boston had the finish, and Arturs Silovs had a night he will want back.

Justin Brazeau gave the Penguins the lead at 9:04 of the first. It didn't hold. Pavel Zacha tied it at 12:07 from David Pastrnak and JJ Peterka, Mark Kastelic tipped one in at 15:04, and Elias Lindholm scored unassisted at 18:57. Boston dominated the first period on expected goals (the quality of the chances), 1.59 to 0.45, and three of those chances turned into goals.

The second was Pittsburgh's period on chances, 1.26 to 0.71, and Nick Robertson's tip at 7:57 made it 3-2. The Penguins didn't get any closer. Zacha scored his second at 14:24, a goal that moved Boston's win chance from 70% to 86%, and Morgan Geekie added another at 16:57. Fraser Minten finished the scoring at 8:39 of the third.

Over 60 minutes the chances were nearly even: 2.78 expected goals for Boston, 2.45 for Pittsburgh, a 56% deserved-to-win share for the Bruins (the share of replays of every shot a team wins). The Penguins attempted 56 shots to Boston's 42 but put only 18 on net, partly because the Bruins blocked 22. Michael DiPietro saved what reached him, 16 of 18.

The scoreboard gap, though, belongs to the goaltending. Silovs allowed six goals on 24 shots, 3.2 more than those shots deserved, and no single number from this game explains the final score better. Zacha had two goals on two shots and added 0.32 wins. Pastrnak had two assists and four shots without scoring himself, and Peterka was stopped on a 20% look in the third, so Boston left some on the table too.

The Bruins have won three straight. The Penguins are winless in four (0-3-1), and this was not a night where the effort was the problem. If you're in Pittsburgh, you'd want to see the next start before deciding how worried to be about the crease, but a 6-2 loss on even chances is the kind that lingers.
headline: Bruins turn ordinary chances into six goals
